I was looking at a Remington 700 in 6.5cr with a Leupold VX-Freedom series, total cost would be about $1,000, which I find appropriate. Thoughts?
That would be a fine set up. I would also look at the Ruger precision rifle and check out vortex optics.

Ruger Precision rifle is a bit pricey, but looks gorgeous. Maybe if I get into it more I'll buy that. The Remington700 is a 3/4 average moa barrel for $700, so it's pretty budget. Looking at vortex optics is fun though, they have some nice options. And their warranty is just as good as Leupold. Very nice.
The new rem 700s have quality control issues so be wary and vortex warranty is way better than Leupold.
If you want 6.5 ballistics cheaply get a 308. and use very light high velocity bullets. Your barrel will last twice as long and your ammo will be cheaper.

You stated that you have AR-15's- you already own the most customizable rifle out there, why not just try a new upper and handloading your ammunition for long distances? There are many sources of information about accurizing the AR-15 online, but they mostly come down to (1) a good trigger, (2) barrel/bolt tolerances- buy as a set, and (3) barrel twist in relation to bullet weight.

My opinion #1(and we all know what that's worth) the easiest method: Build a 24" 5.56 upper and handload heavier VLD bullets for the distances you are looking for. There are a myriad of competitors at Quantico running 5.56 at 1000 yards. Pick your handguard, optics, and accessories (bi-pod, sand bag, and such) carefully. The best thing you can do for accuracy is to replace the stock trigger (FCG) in most AR's with a competition or target trigger pack. Move ahead with other accessories (target stock, hand grip, etc) only after you feel this is what you are looking for and this is the road you want to take. I would look up the 1000 yard service rifle matches at Quantico and see what the majority of competitors are using, as that is generally what works best for the AR platform/bullet weight/barrel twist/optic size. The rest are just personal preferences.

Opinion #2 (take it for what it's worth- not a lot): If the need for something different really strikes your fancy, build or buy an upper in the newer .224 Valkrye or similar target cartridge that will fit your lower receiver.

Opinion #3 (whatever :/ ): get a DPMS LR-10, SR-25, or AR-10 derivative in 7.62x51, 6.5 Cr, or any other long-range cartridge available for this platform. The amount of money you are willing to spend is what will limit your choices in this category. Then you will have between 80 to 90% parts interchangeability with your other AR's (including the triggers! Don't forget the FCG's!). A good setup in 7.62 with a good trigger in a DPMS will come in under the $1000 mark if you shop around. Don't leave out the idea of owning several uppers in case you are not satisfied with 7.62, even though it is the easiest to load for because of (1) availability and sheer size of different makes, types, and weights of projectiles, (2) mass of data downloaded from the internet and in print over the years.

Opinion #4: Get a Remington 700 (I have one also, so I can't bitch too much) and have a rifle that does not share ANY parts with anything else you have, is slow to reload, and just as accurate as a good semi-auto (yes, they are more accurate than an okay semi-auto- a lot has changed in the last decade or so in this field).

I'd look at the Ruger M77 Hawkeye, Controlled round feeding instead of the push feed on the Remington. Remington QC can be spotty, the Rugers come out of the factory top notch.

For around $700.00 though you'd be looking at a wood stocked model, laminated or synthetic stocks push it up to around $1100.00 unless you find a deal.

6.5 Creedmoor do have a shorter barrel life than a .308, but you can't duplicate 6.5 CR ballistics and effectiveness with a .308.
Wood stocks are aesthetic though so that's alright. I'll look into it thanks.

Consider the fact that AR10's are very accurate these days. It's not a surprise for someone to have 1moa out of a 1500 semi auto, and its standard to have 2moa. So you don't necessarily need a bolt action to be accurate. They are just have a better moa/$ ratio. A 500$ bolty will out do a 500$ ar15.

Also, consider that 6.5 wears out barrels faster then .308. Might not matter if you get a bolty, as you will never lose your cool and start magdumping at the end of a day, but it is a consideration for an AR10.

I have a sub 1/2" moa .308 that some gunsmith tweeked for long range and I bought used off him for the price of the Leupold Scope ($1700) alone. BUT, if I was starting fresh (I have multiple .308's) I'd go right to 6.5 Creedemore. The recoil is insanely nice after shooting any .308. I've shot the Ruger Precision, very nice. You can buy a Tikka 6+.5 for under $700 and that's where I'd go if I was on a budget. If I wasn't on a budget, the skys the limit and I'd still go 6.5.
